title: Joel 3:9–16
context: Joel 3:9–16 is a summons to battle that becomes a scene of judgment. Versification: English 2:28–32 is Hebrew 3:1–5, and English chapter 3 is Hebrew chapter 4; this page keeps the WEB numbers. A voice, most likely the prophet speaking for the LORD, calls the nations to prepare for war and come up (3:9–11a). The command “Beat your plowshares into swords” (3:10) reverses the wording of Isaiah 2:4, “They shall beat their swords into plowshares”, and Micah 4:3, “They will beat their swords into plowshares”. Each passage has its own setting: Isaiah and Micah picture nations learning peace under the LORD’s rule, while Joel pictures nations arming for a battle that ends in their own judgment, and readers relate the passages in different ways. In 3:11b the prophet breaks in with a prayer, “Cause your mighty ones to come down there, LORD.” The LORD answers that he will sit in the valley of Jehoshaphat to judge all the surrounding nations, and he calls for the sickle and the wine press, because the harvest is ripe and their wickedness is great (3:12–13). Revelation 14:14–20 takes up harvest and wine press imagery in its own vision of judgment; it is named here without merging the two passages. The prophet then sees multitudes in “the valley of decision”, where the day of the LORD is near (3:14). In context the decision is the LORD’s verdict on the nations he sits to judge, though the phrase is often applied in preaching to a person’s response to God. The darkened sun, moon, and stars repeat 2:10 and echo 2:31, and Joel 3:16 opens with the same words as Amos 1:2, “The LORD will roar from Zion,” though the two books develop the image differently. Historical, typological, and future readings of this gathering are held in both traditions: some readers see judgments on the nations within Israel’s history, some see the coming of Christ and the gospel age as the decisive judgment and harvest, and many see the final judgment at Christ’s return, with premillennial, amillennial, and postmillennial readers relating the scene to Revelation in different ways. None of these is an Arminian or Reformed position as such. On God summoning nations who remain responsible for their hostility, see the Joshua 11:20 and Judges 9:23 boxes rather than a new contrast here. Shared ground: the LORD judges the nations justly and is a refuge to his people (3:16).

verses.text: Proclaim this among the nations: “Prepare for war! Stir up the mighty men. Let all the warriors draw near. Let them come up.
verses.arminianNotes: A voice, most likely the prophet speaking for the LORD, calls the nations to prepare for war and stir up their mighty men. Arminian readers hear an ironic summons: the nations think they are mustering for victory, yet they are coming to their own judgment, and their hostility remains their own choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same irony and stress that the nations come because the LORD summons them, compare Ezekiel 38–39 in its own setting. Shared ground: the nations remain responsible for their hostility even as they are summoned to judgment.

verses.text: Beat your plowshares into swords, and your pruning hooks into spears. Let the weak say, ‘I am strong.’
verses.arminianNotes: “Beat your plowshares into swords” reverses the wording of Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3. Arminian readers see a picture of nations turning every tool of life into a weapon, and they hear a warning about what human pride does with God’s gifts when it sets itself against him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same reversal and read “Let the weak say, ‘I am strong.’” as the false confidence of nations about to be judged. Both traditions name Isaiah and Micah without harmonizing them: those passages picture peace under the LORD’s rule, while Joel pictures a war that ends in judgment.

verses.text: Hurry and come, all you surrounding nations, and gather yourselves together.” Cause your mighty ones to come down there, LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The nations are told to hurry and gather, and then the prophet turns to prayer: “Cause your mighty ones to come down there, LORD.” Arminian readers hear Joel joining his voice to the LORD’s purpose and asking God to act, and they see prayer as a real part of how the day comes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often take the mighty ones as the LORD’s heavenly host, and they see the prophet asking God to do what he has promised to do. On whether prayer changes what God does, see the Joshua 10:14 box; here both traditions read the prayer as faithful agreement with God.

verses.text: “Let the nations arouse themselves, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat; for there I will sit to judge all the surrounding nations.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will sit in the valley of Jehoshaphat to judge all the surrounding nations. Arminian readers see a court scene, with the nations present and their deeds weighed, and they hold that the verdict is just because it answers what the nations have done to God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the picture of the LORD seated as judge, unhurried and sovereign over nations who come up at his word. Both traditions include readers who see this fulfilled in judgments within history, in the gospel age, or at the final judgment, compare Matthew 25:31–32 in its own setting.

verses.text: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD commands the sickle and the treading of the wine press, for the harvest is ripe and their wickedness is great. Arminian readers note that the harvest comes when wickedness has ripened, which fits God’s patience before judgment, as with the Amorites in Genesis 15:16, and leaves room for repentance before that time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the ripened harvest as the appointed time of judgment set by God. Revelation 14:14–20 uses harvest and wine press imagery for judgment in its own vision, and both traditions name it without merging the passages or settling every detail of how they relate.

verses.text: Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision! For the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet sees multitudes in the valley of decision, where the day of the LORD is near. Arminian readers, like many preachers, sometimes apply the phrase to a hearer’s response to God, while recognizing that in context the decision belongs to the LORD, the verdict on the gathered nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the decision here is God’s, the sentence of the judge who sits in 3:12, rather than a choice made by the multitudes. Shared ground: the contextual sense is the LORD’s verdict, and both traditions hold historical, typological, and future readings of the day of the LORD named here.

verses.text: The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.
verses.arminianNotes: The sun and moon are darkened and the stars withdraw their shining, the same words used in 2:10 and an echo of 2:31. Arminian readers read the cosmic signs as the language of the day of the LORD, warning all people to seek him while there is time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the same signs as the traditional imagery of God’s judgment, used also in Isaiah 13:10 and taken up in Matthew 24:29. Readers in both traditions differ over how literally to take the signs, and that difference does not follow Arminian and Reformed lines.

verses.text: The LORD will roar from Zion, and thunder from Jerusalem; and the heavens and the earth will shake; but the LORD will be a refuge to his people, and a stronghold to the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will roar from Zion and thunder from Jerusalem, words that also open Amos 1:2, and heaven and earth will shake. Arminian readers note the turn within the same verse: the LORD who shakes the world is a refuge to his people, and they hear an invitation to take shelter in him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress “the LORD will be a refuge to his people, and a stronghold to the children of Israel” as the security God gives those who belong to him. On whether God’s people are kept to the end, see the 1 Samuel 12:22 box; the LORD as refuge is shared ground.
